title: Mode-selective phonon effects on magnetism and superconductivity in trilayer nickelates
authors: C. Alexander Baum, Jun Zhan, Congcong Le, Ronny Thomale, Xianxin Wu
abstract: The discovery of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in multilayer nickelates has stimulated intense interest, yet the microscopic origins of their correlated states remain debated. Recently the observed isotope effect of the magnetic state in trilayer nickelates highlights the important role of lattice vibrations in shaping these systems. Here, we investigate the impact of electron-phonon coupling (EPC) on magnetism and superconductivity in trilayer nickelates using ab initio and functional renormalization group calculations. We identify out-of-plane oxygen breathing modes with pronounced EPC and construct symmetry-resolved, layer-dependent couplings. Their relative phases across the three layers generate distinct retarded interactions, producing mode-selective enhancement or suppression of spin-density-wave order and $s_\pm$-wave superconductivity. This selectivity arises from screening-mediated spin-phonon interplay across a hierarchy of energy scales: EPC modifies charge screening at higher energies, reshapes magnetic fluctuations at lower energies, and ultimately influences pairing. Selected modes yield negative isotope coefficients for the magnetic state, qualitatively consistent with experiments. Our results establish how interlayer phonons modify electronically driven order and provide a microscopic framework for understanding isotope effects in trilayer nickelates.
summary: This theoretical study uses FRG calculations to map the impact of electron-phonon coupling on magnetism and superconductivity in trilayer nickelates. It finds that the specific out-of-plane oxygen breathing modes create layer-dependent interactions that selectively enhance or suppress competing electronic orders. This establishes a microscopic framework for understanding the observed isotope effects in these high-temperature superconductors.
main_problem: The study investigates how electron-phonon coupling (EPC) influences the competing electronic orders—magnetism (SDW) and superconductivity ($s_\pm$-wave)—in trilayer nickelates.
main_result: The relative phases of EPC across the three layers generate distinct, mode-selective retarded interactions that can enhance or suppress SDW order and superconductivity.
method: The research employs ab initio calculations combined with the Functional Renormalization Group (FRG) formalism to treat phonon-mediated and Coulomb interactions simultaneously.
model_or_system: The system is trilayer nickelates, modeled using a tight-binding approach incorporating various Coulomb interactions. The analysis focuses on out-of-plane oxygen breathing modes which exhibit pronounced EPC.
key_observables: Spin-Density-Wave (SDW) order, $s_\pm$-wave superconducting pairing, isotope coefficients ($\alpha_{SC}, \alpha_{SDW}$), and the Eliashberg spectral function ($\alpha^2F(\omega)$).
important_parameters: High pressure ($P=40 	ext{ GPa}$), specific phonon frequencies (e.g., $553 	ext{ cm}^{-1}, 651 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$), and the relative phases of the EPC across the three layers.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on projecting the full frequency dependence onto static channels within the FRG framework, and the model incorporates specific layer-dependent coupling terms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phonon dispersion and EPC strength, while supplementary figures visualize the evolution of superconducting order parameter components and the calculation of isotope coefficients ($\Delta\Lambda_c$ and $\alpha$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by identifying dominant phonon modes (A1g out-of-plane modes), constructing symmetry-resolved EPC terms, and then using FRG to calculate how these terms modify the electronic interactions, leading to mode-selective predictions for SDW and SC.
why_interesting: The concept of screening-mediated spin–phonon interplay provides a detailed, microscopic mechanism for how lattice vibrations can tune competing electronic orders, which is relevant to understanding quantum criticality in correlated materials.
